draft.title: Inclusion and power
card: Power is the ability to make decisions and shape what others can do. Groups with more power often set the rules about who is included in a society or an organisation.
Rules can be written, such as laws, policies and entry requirements. They can also be unwritten, such as habits about who is listened to or who is seen as belonging.
A group with less power may find the rules shut it out of work, services or decisions. Powerful groups may not notice this, because the rules suit them.
Excluded groups may work to change the rules. They can campaign, protest, vote, take legal action or form their own organisations. This can succeed, but it may take a long time.
draft.remember: Those with more power often write the rules of inclusion, and excluded groups may act to change them.

a.q: Why might a rule about who can take part in a community group exclude some people without the rule makers noticing?
opts: The rule suits those who made it, so they may miss its effect
The rule makers always intend to shut out weaker groups
The rule is a law, and all laws exclude someone
The excluded people have no way to ask for change
a.why: People with power often write rules that fit their own situation, so they may not notice who is left out. The second option is tempting, but the card says only that powerful groups may not notice, not that they always intend exclusion.
a.clue: Think about who the rules were written to suit.

b.q: Residents of a remote town in Western Australia have no local clinic. The health department sets service rules based on population size. The residents form an action group, collect signatures and meet their local member of parliament. What does this show?
opts: An excluded group working to change rules set by others
A powerful group setting rules that include everyone fairly
A group excluding itself by choosing not to use services
A rule that is unwritten and so cannot be challenged
b.why: The department sets the rules, and the residents use a petition and a meeting with their local member to try to change them. The third option is tempting, but the residents are shut out by the service rules, not by their own choice.
b.clue: Who sets the rules, and what is the other group doing about them?
